clue.text: I jettison crop that's failed one screening (13)

indicators.note: a thing that has failed has collapsed out of its proper arrangement, so its letters will not stay in the order they are given

blocks.note: thirteen letters to rearrange: I JETTISON CROP

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grower dumping a ruined harvest, and nothing in it suggests a cinema until the last two words arrive.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinema screening is run from the projection box, so 'one screening' names the person doing the showing rather than the film shown.

clue.text: Epic want solo pared down on one instrument (7)

indicators.note: to pare something is to shave the outside off it, so each word here keeps only what was in its middle

blocks.note: ePIc with its outer letters pared away
wANt loses its shell the same way
sOLo, down to its middle two letters
'one' is the indefinite article A

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a description of a stripped-back epic, but 'pared down' is an instruction, and it governs three words in a row — that repetition is what hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pianola is the self-playing piano worked by a perforated paper roll, so 'instrument' defines it as one member of the keyboard family.

clue.text: Happy to share opinions upon Stoke undergoing an earthquake (9)

indicators.note: an earthquake leaves nothing standing where it stood, and the letters it shakes come back in a different order

blocks.note: the nine letters of UPON STOKE, shaken into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: Stoke puts a real town in the surface and 'upon' reads as a preposition joining it to something — both words are material, which is the hard thing to see.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone outspoken states views frankly and in public, so the definition spells out the readiness to speak that the single word packs in.

clue.text: Record tenants removing walls (5)

indicators.note: the walls of a word are the letters at either end holding the rest in; knock them out and the middle is left standing

blocks.note: people who pay rent are renters

explanation.walkthrough: The first step here is the buried one: the clue never prints the word you are meant to demolish, only a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a figure is to write it into a ledger or register, the bookkeeping sense of the verb rather than walking through a door.

clue.text: Fancy jacket time for everyone on social media site (3)

blocks.note: T is the scientist's symbol for time
a U certificate passes a film for everyone, whatever their age
X is the site that used to be Twitter

explanation.walkthrough: Three abbreviations from three unrelated worlds — physics, film classification and a rebranded website — so no part of the sentence sounds like wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Tux is the short form of tuxedo, the dinner jacket worn with a black tie, and 'fancy' marks it as formalwear rather than everyday dress.

clue.text: Finished performing Tosca in protective gear? (9)

definitions.note: 'Gear' is a mass noun covering any number of garments, so it fairly defines a plural answer without being plural itself.

indicators.note: an opera exists to be staged, and every staging puts the same material up in a different arrangement

blocks.note: when something is finished it is over
the five letters of Puccini's opera, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished performing' reads as one phrase about the end of a run, and that false join is exactly the seam the clue wants you to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcoat is the heavy outer coat worn over everything else against the weather, so the definition names them by what they shield you from.

clue.text: Buddhist chant supports old Ugandan saying (5)

indicators.note: whatever supports a thing stands underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means further along the answer

blocks.note: Idi Amin, Uganda's dictator in the 1970s
om is the syllable chanted in Buddhist and Hindu practice

explanation.walkthrough: Idi Amin is the setter's standing source for three letters whenever Uganda turns up — worth filing away with the rest of the crossword's cast.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed turn of phrase that means more than its words do, and 'saying' is the everyday term for such a phrase.

clue.text: Internet troublemaker initially explains young loony's off this? (7)

definitions.note: The definition is not a synonym: it is an idiom with the answer knocked out of it, so what is wanted is the object a loony is said to be off.

indicators.note: initially means at the very outset, so only the letter each word starts with is wanted

blocks.note: a troll is someone who stirs up trouble online
the opening letter of each of those two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Off one's trolley' is the phrase the question mark points at, so the definition is a whole idiom with its noun missing rather than a word for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Off one's trolley means out of one's mind, so TROLLEY is the noun that idiom hangs on rather than any synonym for madness.

clue.text: Slow at thinking, displays a bit of power (4)

indicators.note: to display something is to have it in plain view, which is where a hidden word always is once you read letters instead of words

blocks.note: lying across sloW AT Thinking

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the mismatch: a phrase about being dim is where a unit of power turns out to be sitting. James Watt gave the unit its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A watt is the SI unit of power, so 'a bit of power' means a measured quantity of the physical stuff, not a share of influence.

clue.text: How setter might contact boss on a mobile application (4,6)

blocks.note: to text somebody is to send them a message
the setter's boss is the crossword editor, who commissions and checks the puzzle
surface only — the phone is where texting happens and it contributes no letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' means the person who wrote this crossword, and their boss really is an editor: a rare clue whose wordplay is autobiographical.
explanation.definitionFit: A text editor is the bare program you type and save plain text in, so 'application' defines it by the kind of software it is.

clue.text: On air, was a show host judged against somebody else? (8)

indicators.note: on air means broadcast, so the words are being spoken rather than printed and the sound is what counts

blocks.note: to compere is to host a show, so this is COMPERED; say it aloud and you write the other spelling

explanation.walkthrough: A compere is the person who introduces the acts, from the French for godfather — two spellings that sound identical and mean nothing like each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To compare is to set one thing beside another and weigh them up, which is the past-tense verb the definition describes at length.

clue.text: Small detachments of troops severely criticised about Italy’s uprising (7)

indicators.note: about here means round, in the sense of a fence about a field: one piece is wrapped round another rather than set beside it
an uprising rises, and a down entry read upwards from its foot runs the other way

blocks.note: to slate something is to criticise it savagely; it opens between the L and the A
I is Italy's international vehicle registration letter

explanation.walkthrough: It takes a passenger and is then read upwards. On the surface, an uprising in Italy is simply the news.
explanation.definitionFit: In army usage a detail is a small party told off for a particular duty, a sense of the word that survives mainly in the military and in crosswords.

clue.text: Go along with firm parliamentarian - lobby must be eviscerated (6)

indicators.note: to eviscerate is to take the innards out, which leaves a word standing as an empty shell

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a Member of Parliament
L…Y is all that is left of LOBBY once the middle is out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lobby' is chosen with care — it is the parliamentary word for the corridor where members are buttonholed, so the surface never breaks character.
explanation.definitionFit: To comply is to do what a rule or a request demands, the sense of 'go along with' that means fall into line rather than accompany.

clue.text: Bust rioting punk brat (8)

indicators.note: a riot leaves nothing where it was, so the letters caught up in it come back in another order

blocks.note: the eight letters of PUNK BRAT, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: Three words and nothing else. Short clues are often the hardest, because there is no surface to tell you which end the definition is at.
explanation.definitionFit: Bust is the colloquial word for having gone broke, so it matches the legal state of being unable to pay what you owe.

clue.text: Liberated a French church Diane renovated (9)

indicators.note: renovating a building keeps the material and rearranges it, and a name can be rebuilt the same way

blocks.note: 'a' in French is UN
CH is the standard abbreviation for church
the five letters of DIANE, rebuilt

explanation.walkthrough: 'A French' is the setter asking for the French word for 'a' rather than describing anything Gallic — a construction worth recognising on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To unchain is literally to release from chains, so 'liberated' is the same past participle in its plainest sense of set free.

clue.text: Haul a weary ass regularly, or every time? (6)

indicators.note: at regular intervals — take a letter, skip a letter, and keep to that beat all the way along

blocks.note: every second letter of hAuL A wEaRy AsS

explanation.walkthrough: The donkey is scenery. What matters is that the phrase was built letter by letter to land on the answer, small words counted in with the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Every time' is the frequency sense of the answer — on each occasion, without exception — rather than the 'for ever' sense the word also carries.

clue.text: Colonist's religious outfit - tiny according to Spooner (6,3)

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner's trick was to trade the opening sounds of two words, so his version of a phrase has them swapped over

blocks.note: a burka is the religious garment; it hands its B over and takes a W in exchange
tiny is wee, and it collects the B the first word gave up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonist' is the misdirection — it suggests settlers and empire, when the colony in question is a hive.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker bee belongs to the colony that fills a hive, so 'colonist' names it by the community it lives in rather than by settling abroad.

clue.text: Husband about to crash photo of speech (6)

indicators.note: to crash a party is to get inside it uninvited, so these letters push in where they were not asked

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
a book about cats is a book on cats
a photo is a pic, and it splits P…IC to let the other two in

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' meaning ON is worth banking — it turns up constantly — and here it also keeps the surface reading as a husband barging into a picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Phonic means relating to speech sounds, as in the phonics children learn to read by, so 'of speech' is the adjective's technical sense.

clue.text: European condition found in that woman's cows, ... (7)

indicators.note: found in says where the pieces end up: inside the word that follows, not alongside it

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
an 'if' is a condition attached to a promise
what belongs to that woman is hers; it opens up after the H

explanation.walkthrough: 'Condition' as IF is the step to spot. Everything else reads as an ordinary sentence about somebody's livestock, which is what makes it hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A heifer is a young cow that has not yet had a calf, so 'cows' defines the answer by the wider category it belongs to.

clue.text: Carve manger in Xmas decoration, avoiding the edges (8)

indicators.note: 'in' is positional here: the manger is put inside the longer word rather than next to it
the edges of a word are its first and last letters, and this one is to be taken without them

blocks.note: the decoration is TINSEL; without its edges it reads INSE, and it opens to take a passenger
a crib is the manger in a nativity scene

explanation.walkthrough: The crib and the tinsel keep the surface entirely Christmassy, so the two instructions buried in it — go inside, drop the edges — read as decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: To inscribe is to cut letters into stone or metal, so 'carve' is the engraving sense of the verb rather than shaping wood.

clue.text: ... chickens, bats and man out of sorts (7)

indicators.note: sorts are the sorted pieces of type in a printer's case, so out of sorts is out of order

blocks.note: BATS and MAN, seven letters shuffled together

explanation.walkthrough: The clue finishes the sentence 18 down started, and 'bats' looks like an instruction to shuffle in its own right. It isn't — it is material.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a miniature breed of domestic fowl, so 'chickens' defines them by species and says nothing about the famous small size.

clue.text: Roman street artist swallows good drug (6)

indicators.note: to swallow something is to take it inside you, so a piece disappears within the letters already assembled

blocks.note: via is Latin, and modern Italian, for a road
G is the standard abbreviation for good
a Royal Academician, the crossword's usual artist

explanation.walkthrough: RA for artist and G for good are two of the abbreviations that come up most often; 'Roman street artist' is three separate pieces standing in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Viagra is the trade name of the pill prescribed for erectile dysfunction, so 'drug' defines it by example — one medicine, not the class.

clue.text: Look around you for light dressing (5)

indicators.note: around means wrapped right round the outside, so the shorter piece finishes up in the middle

blocks.note: to look steadily is to gaze; it opens between the A and the Z
U is the text-message spelling of 'you'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Look around you' is a complete instruction in ordinary English, which is why it slides past — and the setter means it letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauze is the thin open-weave cotton laid over a wound, so 'light dressing' names it by its weight and its medical use.

clue.text: Encourage onboard medical professionals (8)

indicators.note: being aboard a vessel means being inside it, so the ship closes around whatever it is carrying

blocks.note: a steamship is SS, and it splits S…S around its passengers
to urge somebody on is to encourage them

explanation.walkthrough: One word has to be read as two doing two jobs: the ON that completes the phrasal verb, and the vessel that wraps itself round the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon is the doctor who operates rather than prescribes, so 'medical professionals' defines them as one branch of the profession.

clue.text: Correct audio for ceremony (5)

indicators.note: audio is sound rather than print, so the clue wants the word listened to instead of read

blocks.note: a ceremony is a rite; spoken aloud it arrives as the other spelling

explanation.walkthrough: English keeps three of this sound in play — rite, wright and write — so it is the crossing letters, not the ear, that decide which the grid wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Right here means accurate, not the opposite of left nor an entitlement, so 'correct' picks one adjective sense out of several.

clue.text: Ordering mashed quince in shells of Senegalese nutmeg (10)

indicators.note: mashing a thing breaks it up and leaves the pieces in no particular order
'in' says the broken-up letters go inside what follows rather than beside it
a shell is a hard outside with nothing left within, so only the first and last letters of each word survive

blocks.note: the shell of SenegalesE
the six letters of QUINCE, mashed
the shell of NutmeG

explanation.walkthrough: Two different words supply the shell, one pair of letters each, which is what makes the container hard to see behind an entirely edible surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sequencing is putting things one after another into a sequence, which is what ordering means when it is arrangement rather than buying goods.

clue.text: Cretan's height of impertinence, disregarding Athenian's introductions (3)

indicators.note: an introduction comes first, so each word is represented by the letter it opens with

blocks.note: the opening letters of those three words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disregarding' looks like an instruction to drop something and is really fodder — the initials run straight through it, which is the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Ida is the highest peak in Crete and the cave where Zeus was said to be raised, so 'Cretan's height' names the mountain.

clue.text: Heartless, trite ancient god (4)

indicators.note: the heart of a word is the letter at its centre, and a heartless word has had that letter taken out

blocks.note: something trite is banal

explanation.walkthrough: Baal is the Canaanite god the Old Testament rails against, and the comma after the first word invites you to read it as describing a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Baal was the storm and fertility god worshipped across the ancient Levant, so 'ancient god' places him by era and by role.

clue.text: Stan's deaf - Tess possibly shows loyalty (13)

indicators.note: possibly flags one arrangement of these letters among the many available, and not the arrangement printed

blocks.note: the thirteen letters of STANS DEAF TESS, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' is a mild anagram signal that reads as ordinary hedging, and the two names exist only to hand over letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadfastness is unwavering constancy to a person or a cause, which is what loyalty amounts to once it is tested over time.
